statement: Floor tiles are equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons, all with the same side length. Which set of tiles can fit together around a single point, with no gaps and no overlaps?

choices.text: one hexagon, two squares and one triangle

choices.misconception: I gave the triangle a corner of 90 degrees, the same as a square, so the corners seemed to add to 360.
I took a hexagon's corner to be 135 degrees, so 135 + 135 + 90 seemed to make 360.
I treated the hexagon's corner as a right angle, so four right angles seemed to fill the point.
I took a triangle's corner to be 45 degrees, half a right angle, so four of them and two squares seemed to make 360.

hints: What must the corners meeting at one point add up to?
The corners around a point must total exactly 360 degrees. Find the corner angle of each kind of tile, then add up each set and see which one makes exactly 360.
A triangle's corner is 60 degrees, a square's is 90 and a hexagon's is 120. Add each set: only one reaches exactly 360.

solutions.reliable: The angles meeting at a point make a full turn, 360 degrees. The corners are: triangle 60, square 90, hexagon 120 (a regular hexagon splits into 6 equilateral triangles, and each of its corners is made of two 60-degree angles). Now add: three squares and a triangle make 330; two hexagons and a square make 330; a hexagon and three squares make 390; four triangles and two squares make 420; a hexagon, two squares and a triangle make 120 + 180 + 60 = 360. The transferable idea: tiles fit around a point exactly when their corner angles add to 360.
solutions.elegant: Measure every corner in triangle corners: a triangle is worth 1, a square 1 and a half, a hexagon 2, and a full turn 6. A hexagon (2), two squares (3) and a triangle (1) make exactly 6; every other set misses.

whyOnTest: Tiling questions come down to one fact, that angles around a point make 360 degrees, plus knowing the corner of each regular shape.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
